title: Learning exposes limits of predicting new running injuries
summary: An Explainable Boosting Machine analyzed surveys and running logs from 643 marathon trainees, holding out all observations from test runners. Prediction was much weaker among runners not already modifying training: AUROC was 0.673 and precision-recall area 0.077, compared with 0.873 and 0.521 across all runner-weeks. Outcomes were self-reported training-limiting injuries; the study did not demonstrate prevention or real-time clinical benefit.
ai_technology: Explainable Boosting Machine; boosted generalized additive model
organization: Hospital for Special Surgery; Weill Cornell Medicine

source_review.scope: Primary relevant model Methods, Results and limitations; exact primary identity and current primary PubMed correction/retraction relationships checked.

evidence.tested: Runner-grouped 80:20 train/test evaluation of upcoming-week self-reported injury using only earlier surveys/logs.
evidence.unknown: External replication, medically confirmed injury outcomes and prevention benefit remain unestablished; persistent existing injury accounts for much overall predictive performance.
evidence.ai_role: Boosted shallow trees learn nonlinear additive relationships between prior training/symptom measures and subsequent weekly injury status.
